text:
Two equally consistent readings fit all the known tasks, and they give opposite buttons on every input. My predictions are a 50/50 pick between them.

**Which bit each Y component reads** (found from the examples)

- **Y2 is bit 3.** In X3-Y2-Z2, button 3 appears exactly when bit 3 is 0 in both stimuli. So X3 is either "neither" (true gives 3) or "at least one" (true gives 1).
- **Y1 is bit 4.**
  - In X5-Y1-Z2, button 1 appears exactly when bit 4 is 0 in both. So either X5 is "neither" and Z2 gives 1 when true, or X5 is "at least one" and Z2 gives 3 when true.
  - In X6-Y1-Z2, button 3 appears exactly when bit 4 is the same in both. So either X6 is "same" and Z2 gives 3 when true, or X6 is "exactly one" and Z2 gives 1 when true.
  - In X5-Y1-Z3, button 0 appears exactly when bit 4 is 0 in both.
- **Y4 is bit 1.** In X6-Y4-Z3, button 1 appears exactly when bit 1 is the same in both.
- **Y3 is bit 2.** In X4-Y3-Z4, button 3 appears exactly when bit 2 is 1 in both. So X4 is either "both" (true gives 3) or "not both" (true gives 2).

**The two global assignments**

Both fit every example and keep different versions of a kind different:

| | Z2 when true | X3 | X5 | X6 | Z3 when true |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 3 | neither | at least one | same | 1 |
| B | 1 | at least one | neither | exactly one | 0 |

In both A and B, X4 can be either "both" or "not both". Nothing in the examples connects X4 to Z2.

**What this means for the new task, X4-Y3-Z2**

The new task looks at bit 2. The four combinations collapse into two possible answers:

- **A with "both", or B with "not both":** button 3 when bit 2 is 1 in both stimuli, otherwise button 1.
- **A with "not both", or B with "both":** the reverse, swapping 1 and 3 on every input.

The examples don't settle which is right, so I picked the first, which makes my confidence 0.5. Only inputs 9 (1110 1100) and 13 (1110 1111) have bit 2 equal to 1 in both stimuli, so they get button 3 and the rest get button 1.

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: 0, 1, 2, or 3. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> 2` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is 2.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
